title: Ghost Stories of an Antiquary
description: The founding book of the modern English ghost story: 'Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad' and the antiquarian terror.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'Canon Alberic's Scrap-Book', 'Lost Hearts', 'The Mezzotint', 'The Ash-tree', 'Number 13', 'Count Magnus', 'Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad' and 'The Treasure of Abbot Thomas' — stories of scholars, manuscripts and things that should not be disturbed.
narrative_structure: Eight stories, each framed by a document, a manuscript or a scholarly discovery.
principal_characters: Professor Parkins; Canon Alberic; Count Magnus; Mr Williams; Stephen Elliott
historical_context: The English cathedral towns and country houses of the 1890s, the antiquarian scholarship of the period, and the Christmas ghost-story tradition.
literary_significance: Ghost Stories of an Antiquary founded the modern English ghost story: its antiquarian frame, its exact topography and its withheld apparitions made it the model for the genre, and 'Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad' is the most famous ghost story in English.

title: A Thin Ghost and Others
description: James's third collection: 'The Rose Garden', 'The Tractate Middoth' and the quietest of the antiquarian terrors.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Rose Garden', 'The Tractate Middoth', 'The Residence at Whitminster', 'The Diary of Mr Poynter' and 'An Episode of Cathedral History' — stories of country houses, libraries and the dead who will not stay buried.
narrative_structure: Five stories in the antiquarian frame, each with a document or an object at its centre.
principal_characters: Mr Garrett; Mr Dunning; Mr Lake; the Dean
historical_context: The English country house and cathedral close of the 1900s, and the postwar taste for the antiquarian ghost story.
literary_significance: A Thin Ghost and Others is James's quietest and most accomplished collection: 'The Tractate Middoth' is one of his finest stories, and the collection shows the master of the antiquarian ghost story at the height of his craft.

title: The Willows
description: The greatest supernatural story of the outdoors: two men, a canoe, and the willows of the Danube.
plot_or_argument: Two friends canoe down the Danube and camp on a remote island overgrown with willows, where they become aware of a vast, hostile, non-human presence that hunts them through the night and across the river.
narrative_structure: A first-person narrative of a single night on the river.
principal_characters: The narrator; the Swede; the willows; the unseen presence
literary_form: Novella (in The Listener and Other Stories)
historical_context: The Danube of the 1900s, the river travel of the period, and Blackwood's own canoe trips in Europe.
literary_significance: The Willows is the greatest supernatural story of the outdoors and one of the finest ghost stories in English: its terror comes from the landscape itself, and Lovecraft called it the finest supernatural story in English literature.

title: The Great God Pan
description: The most influential English horror story of the 1890s: an experiment on the brain that opens the way to the pagan god.
plot_or_argument: Dr Raymond's experiment on a young woman opens her mind to the god Pan and destroys her; years later her daughter Helen Vaughan spreads corruption and death through London society until she is hunted down and destroyed by her father's friends.
narrative_structure: A novella in eight sections, told through documents and testimony.
principal_characters: Dr Raymond; Helen Vaughan; Villiers; Austin; Clarke
historical_context: The decadent London of the 1890s, the new psychical research, and the pagan revival of the period.
literary_significance: The Great God Pan is the most influential English horror story of the 1890s: its theme of the pagan survival and its suggestion of unspeakable horror made it the model for the modern weird tale, and Lovecraft and Stephen King both acknowledge it.

title: The Hill of Dreams
description: The finest decadent novel in English: a young writer's ecstasy and destruction in the Welsh hills and London.
plot_or_argument: Lucian Taylor, a Welsh clergyman's son, becomes a writer, escapes to London and lives in poverty and ecstasy, caught between the Roman past of his native hills and the visions of his own imagination, until his mind and body fail.
narrative_structure: A novel in five parts, from the Welsh childhood to the London collapse.
principal_characters: Lucian Taylor; Annie Morgan; the rector; the London landlady
historical_context: Wales and London at the end of the nineteenth century, the decadent movement, and the poverty of the literary hack.
literary_significance: The Hill of Dreams is the finest decadent novel in English and Machen's masterpiece: its prose ecstasies, its Welsh landscape and its portrait of the artist destroyed by his own vision made it one of the great novels of the 1890s.

title: The Rising of the Moon
description: Lady Gregory's most famous one-act play: a policeman, a ballad singer and the choice of loyalty.
plot_or_argument: On a quay in a west of Ireland town, a sergeant of the Royal Irish Constabulary is posted to watch for an escaped rebel; a ragged ballad singer sits down to talk with him, and by the end the sergeant has let the man go, knowing who he is.
narrative_structure: A single scene on a quay, in one act.
principal_characters: The Sergeant; the Ragged Man; two policemen
historical_context: The west of Ireland at the turn of the century, the Land War's aftermath and the Irish revolutionary movement.
literary_significance: The Rising of the Moon is Lady Gregory's most famous play and the finest one-act play of the Irish revival: its stagecraft, its dialogue and its quiet treatment of loyalty and nation made it a permanent part of the repertory.

title: Spreading the News
description: The comedy that opened the Abbey Theatre: a rumour in a fair-day village and a magistrate's court in uproar.
plot_or_argument: At the fair in the village of Cloon, a casual remark about a man with a hayfork sets off a rumour of murder that spreads through the whole village and ends in a magistrate's court, with every witness contradicting the last.
narrative_structure: A single act, set at the fair and in the court.
principal_characters: Bartley Fallon; Mrs Fallon; Jack Smith; the Magistrate; Mrs Tarpey; Shawn Early
historical_context: The west of Ireland, the petty sessions court and the oral culture of the village.
literary_significance: Spreading the News is the comedy that opened the Abbey Theatre on 27 December 1904 and one of the funniest one-act plays in English: its anatomy of rumour made it Lady Gregory's most performed work.

title: The Workhouse Ward
description: The finest comic one-act play in Irish English: two old men in a workhouse who cannot live together and cannot live apart.
plot_or_argument: Two old paupers, Michael Miskell and Mrs Donohue's brother, quarrel endlessly in the workhouse ward; when Michael's sister offers to take him away, he refuses to leave his enemy, and the two settle back into their quarrel.
narrative_structure: A single act in the workhouse ward.
principal_characters: Michael Miskell; Mrs Donohue's brother; the Warden; the Matron
historical_context: The Irish workhouse at the end of the nineteenth century and the poverty of the rural west.
literary_significance: The Workhouse Ward is the finest comic one-act play in Irish English and Lady Gregory's masterpiece: its two old men quarrelling made a permanent comic archetype and the play remains in the Abbey repertory.

title: Hay Fever
description: Coward's first great comedy: the Bliss family and their four weekend guests.
plot_or_argument: Judith Bliss, a retired actress, and her novelist husband David, their children Simon and Sorel, and the writer Myra Arundel entertain four weekend guests at their country house, each of whom has been invited by a different member of the family; by Sunday lunchtime all four guests have fled.
narrative_structure: Three acts, a Saturday evening, Sunday morning and Sunday afternoon.
principal_characters: Judith Bliss; David Bliss; Sorel Bliss; Simon Bliss; Myra Arundel; Richard Greatham; Jackie Coryton; Sandy Tyrell
historical_context: The English country house of the 1920s and the theatrical family at its centre.
literary_significance: Hay Fever is Coward's first great comedy and one of the funniest plays in English: its portrait of the self-absorbed theatrical family made it a permanent part of the repertory and established Coward's style.

title: Private Lives
description: The wittiest comedy of the period: divorced lovers on adjacent honeymoons in the south of France.
plot_or_argument: Elyot and Amanda, divorced for five years, meet on the terrace of a hotel at Deauville while on honeymoon with their new spouses; within a day they have abandoned them and run away together to Paris, where their old quarrels begin again.
narrative_structure: Three acts, in a Deauville hotel and a Paris flat.
principal_characters: Elyot Chase; Amanda Prynne; Sibyl Chase; Victor Prynne; Louise
historical_context: Deauville and Paris in 1930, the international smart set, and the new informality of postwar manners.
literary_significance: Private Lives is the wittiest comedy of the period and Coward's masterpiece: its dialogue, its portrait of the incompatible couple and its invention of the modern comedy of manners made it the most performed English comedy of the century.

title: Blithe Spirit
description: The longest-running comedy in the English theatre: a séance brings back a novelist's first wife.
plot_or_argument: Charles Condomine, a novelist, invites the medium Madame Arcati to a séance to gather material; the ghost of his first wife Elvira appears, visible only to him, and sets out to destroy his second marriage — until a second accident brings Ruth back as well.
narrative_structure: Three acts, in the Condomines' living room.
principal_characters: Charles Condomine; Elvira; Ruth; Madame Arcati; Dr Bradman; Mrs Bradman; Edith
historical_context: An English country house during the Second World War, and the vogue for spiritualism between the wars.
literary_significance: Blithe Spirit was written in six days in 1941 and became the longest-running comedy in the English theatre: its technical brilliance and its portrait of the haunted household made it Coward's most popular play.

title: Present Laughter
description: Coward's self-portrait: a matinee idol besieged by his admirers on the eve of a world tour.
plot_or_argument: Garry Essendine, a famous actor, is about to leave for Africa on tour when his household is invaded by a young admirer, a predatory novelist, his estranged wife and his producer; the comedy is his attempt to keep his life and his ego intact.
narrative_structure: Three acts, in Garry's flat in London.
principal_characters: Garry Essendine; Liz Essendine; Monica Reed; Daphne Stillington; Fred; Roland Maule; Morris Dixon
historical_context: The London theatre of 1939 and the world of the West End star.
literary_significance: Present Laughter is Coward's self-portrait and one of his finest comedies: its portrait of the actor's vanity and its brilliant construction made it a permanent part of the repertory.

title: Design for Living
description: The most scandalous comedy of the thirties: a woman, a painter and a playwright who cannot choose between them.
plot_or_argument: Gilda, an interior decorator, lives with the painter Otto and the playwright Leo in turn and at once; the three travel from Paris to London to New York, and the play ends with all three together, a ménage à trois presented as the only honest arrangement.
narrative_structure: Three acts (Paris, London, New York).
principal_characters: Gilda; Otto; Leo; Ernest Friedman; Grace Torrence; Helen Carver
historical_context: Paris, London and New York in the early 1930s, and the sexual politics of the smart set.
literary_significance: Design for Living was the most scandalous comedy of the thirties and Coward's most daring treatment of sexual freedom: its wit and its refusal to moralise made it the definitive play of the period's sexual politics.

title: Cavalcade
description: Coward's pageant of English life from the Boer War to 1930: the Marryot family and the century.
plot_or_argument: The play follows the Marryot family and their servants, the Bridges, from New Year's Eve 1899 to New Year's Eve 1929, through the Boer War, the Titanic, the First World War and the General Strike, ending with a vision of England's future.
narrative_structure: Two parts, twenty-two scenes, from 1899 to 1929.
principal_characters: Jane Marryot; Robert Marryot; Alfred Bridges; Ellen Bridges; Fanny Bridges; Joe Marryot; Edward Marryot
historical_context: The Boer War, the Titanic, the First World War, the General Strike and the Depression, seen from a single London household.
literary_significance: Cavalcade was the greatest popular success of the thirties' theatre and the period's most ambitious attempt to put the national experience on the stage: its film version won the Academy Award for Best Picture, and its final scene remains one of the most famous in English drama.

title: The Vortex
description: The play that made Coward famous: a mother, her lover and her son in a Chelsea flat.
plot_or_argument: Florence Lancaster, a fashionable woman of forty, takes a young lover; her son Nicky, a composer, returns from Paris with his own secrets, and the two confront each other in a scene of drug-taking and accusation that shocked the West End.
narrative_structure: Three acts, in the Lancester flat and a country house.
principal_characters: Florence Lancaster; Nicky Lancaster; Tom Veryan; Bunty Mainwaring; Helen Saville; Pauncefort Quentin
historical_context: Chelsea and the London smart set of 1924, and the generation that had come through the war.
literary_significance: The Vortex made Coward famous overnight and changed the English theatre: its treatment of drug addiction and sexual hypocrisy in a drawing-room comedy opened the way for the serious play of modern manners.

title: Last and First Men
description: The most ambitious future history ever written: the eighteen species of humanity over two billion years.
plot_or_argument: An unnamed narrator of the last human species tells the history of humanity from the twentieth century to the end of the solar system: the First Men destroy themselves, the Second Men rise in Patagonia, the Martian invasion, the Great Brains, the Flying Men and the Last Men on Neptune, and finally the death of the sun.
narrative_structure: A future history in sixteen chapters, narrated from the last age of humanity.
principal_characters: The narrator; the First Men; the Second Men; the Martians; the Last Men
historical_context: The astronomy and biology of 1930, the aftermath of the First World War, and the philosophy of the species.
literary_significance: Last and First Men is the most ambitious future history ever written and the founding text of the cosmic novel: its scale and its philosophical seriousness gave science fiction a literature it had never had.

title: Star Maker
description: The greatest cosmological vision in English fiction: a journey through the inhabited universe to the creator.
plot_or_argument: A man sitting on a hill at night is carried out of his body and travels through the universe, visiting other worlds, joining his mind with the Other Men of the galactic community, and finally confronting the Star Maker himself, the artist of the cosmos.
narrative_structure: A cosmic journey in fifteen chapters, from the hill to the creator.
principal_characters: The narrator; the Other Men; the Star Maker
historical_context: The astronomy and cosmology of the 1930s, and the philosophical and religious speculation of the interwar years.
literary_significance: Star Maker is the greatest cosmological vision in English fiction: its tour of the universe, its galactic community and its final vision of the creator made it the most philosophically ambitious work of science fiction ever written, and it influenced Arthur C. Clarke and every cosmic writer since.

title: Odd John: A Story Between Jest and Earnest
description: The first serious study of the superman: a boy with a mind beyond the human, and the colony he founds.
plot_or_argument: John Wainwright, born to ordinary parents, is a mutant with an intelligence beyond the human; the narrator, a writer, becomes his friend and biographer as John gathers other mutants, founds a colony on an island, and finally confronts the human race.
narrative_structure: A biography by the narrator, in twenty-one chapters.
principal_characters: John Wainwright; the narrator; Pax; the mutants of the island
historical_context: The 1930s, the eugenics debate, and the philosophy of the superman.
literary_significance: Odd John is the first serious study of the superman in English fiction: it gave the theme its moral seriousness and its tragedy, and it remains the finest treatment of the mutant in the genre.

title: Sirius: A Fantasy of Love and Discord
description: Stapledon's finest novel: a dog given human intelligence, and the loneliness of the creature between species.
plot_or_argument: Sirius, a puppy of the Great Dane breed, is given human intelligence by a scientist, and grows up between the human and the animal worlds: he loves a woman, plays music, writes a book, and is destroyed by the hatred of the humans who cannot accept him.
narrative_structure: A biography in fourteen chapters, from puppyhood to death.
principal_characters: Sirius; Thomas Trelone; Plaxy Trelone; Elizabeth Trelone
historical_context: North Wales in the 1930s, the biology of the period and the war years.
literary_significance: Sirius is Stapledon's finest novel and the most moving book in the scientific romance: its study of a creature between two species and its treatment of love and loneliness made it the most humane work of his career.

title: Dangerous Corner
description: The play that introduced the time-slip to the English stage: a dinner party unpicks a death, then lives it again.
plot_or_argument: At a dinner party at the Caplans' country house, a remark about a cigarette box leads to the uncovering of the truth about the death of Martin Caplen; at the height of the revelation, the clock strikes and the play begins again, and the guests choose not to pursue the truth.
narrative_structure: Three acts, the second a repetition of the first with another outcome.
principal_characters: Robert Caplan; Freda Caplan; Olwen Peel; Betty Whitehouse; Gordon Whitehouse; Charles Trevor Stanton; Maude Mockridge
historical_context: The English country house of 1932 and the prosperous middle-class family.
literary_significance: Dangerous Corner was Priestley's first play and the first to use the time-slip device: its second chance and its moral about the danger of truth made it the founding work of Priestley's theatre of time.
